name: Notre-Dame de Paris
info: Notre-Dame de Paris is the Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité in Paris, begun in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and largely completed by 1260, and a recognised symbol of the city and of France.

facts.made: Begun by Maurice de Sully, bishop of Paris, and continued under Eudes de Sully by master builders whose names have been lost, then by Jean de Chelles, Pierre de Montreuil and later masters; restored in the 19th century by Jean-Baptiste Lassus and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc
facts.form: A Gothic cathedral and basilica with a choir, nave, transepts, chapels and two west towers 69 metres high, using rib vaults, flying buttresses, three rose windows and richly sculpted portals
facts.where: On the Île de la Cité, an island in the Seine, in the 4th arrondissement of Paris; owned by the French state and used by the Catholic Church
facts.known: pioneering rib vaults and flying buttresses; the rose windows; the sculpture of the west façade and the gargoyles and chimeras; the relics of the Passion, including the crown of thorns; the great organ and its bells; Victor Hugo's novel; the fire of 2019

t: Maurice de Sully had the earlier cathedral demolished and began a much larger Gothic church in 1163; four phases of building under two bishops brought it largely to completion by 1260.

The building was stripped and damaged in the French Revolution, fell into disrepair, and was restored between 1844 and 1864 by Viollet-le-Duc after Victor Hugo's novel of 1831 drew attention to its state.
A fire on 15 April 2019 destroyed the flèche and the oak roof beams; the main structure survived, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
dyk: In 2023 archaeologists found thousands of iron staples in the cathedral, some dating from the early 1160s, and concluded that Notre-Dame is the first known Gothic cathedral where iron was used massively to bind stones.
ev: Construction began with the laying of the cornerstone in the presence of King Louis VII and Pope Alexander III
The west rose window, the first and smallest of the three roses, was made
The ten-year-old Henry VI of England was crowned king of France in the cathedral
During the French Revolution the cathedral was rededicated to the Cult of Reason, and its treasures were destroyed or plundered
Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of the French in the cathedral on 2 December
Jean-Baptiste Lassus and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc were appointed to a restoration that lasted until 1864
A fire destroyed the flèche and the roof timbers
The restored cathedral reopened in a ceremony on 7 December

sections.origins:
It is believed that before the arrival of Christianity in France a Gallo-Roman temple dedicated to Jupiter stood on the site of Notre-Dame, on the Île de la Cité, an island in the Seine. Evidence for this includes the Pillar of the Boatmen, discovered beneath the cathedral. In the 4th or 5th century a large early Christian church, the Cathedral of Saint Étienne, was built there close to the royal palace. It was roughly half the size of the later Notre-Dame, 70 metres long, and was divided into nave and four aisles by marble columns and decorated with mosaics. The last church before the cathedral was a Romanesque remodelling of Saint-Étienne, which was found to be unfit for the growing population of Paris.

In 1160 the bishop of Paris, Maurice de Sully, decided to build a new and much larger church. He summarily demolished the earlier cathedral and recycled its materials. He decided that the new church should be built in the Gothic style, which had been inaugurated at the royal abbey of Saint Denis in the late 1130s. The chronicler Jean de Saint-Victor recorded that construction began between 24 March and 25 April 1163 with the laying of the cornerstone in the presence of King Louis VII and Pope Alexander III.
sections.content:
The cathedral is dedicated to the Virgin Mary, "Our Lady", and is considered one of the finest examples of French Gothic architecture. Several attributes set it apart from the earlier Romanesque style: its pioneering use of the rib vault and flying buttress, its enormous and colourful rose windows, and the naturalism and abundance of its sculptural decoration. The two towers are 69 metres high, and the west rose window is 9.6 metres across. The transept roses are larger and contain a greater proportion of glass, because the new system of buttresses made the nave walls thinner and stronger.

The Gothic cathedral was a liber pauperum, a "poor people's book", covered with sculpture that illustrated biblical stories for the many parishioners who could not read. The tympanum of the central west portal shows the Last Judgment, the right portal the coronation of the Virgin and the left portal the lives of saints important to Parisians, particularly Saint Anne. All the sculpture on the façades was originally painted and gilded. Grotesques such as the chimera and the strix stood as symbols of the evil that threatened those who did not follow the church's teaching, while the gargoyles, added about 1240, were rain spouts that threw water clear of the walls.
sections.making:
Four phases of construction took place under bishops Maurice de Sully and Eudes de Sully, who were not related, according to masters whose names have been lost. The first phase built the choir and its two ambulatories; according to Robert of Torigni the choir was completed in 1177 and the high altar was consecrated on 19 May 1182. The second phase, from 1182 to 1190, built the nave to the height of the clerestories, and from 1190 the bases of the façade were put in place. Four-part rather than six-part rib vaults made the roofs stronger and allowed them to be higher. The western façade was largely built by the time of Eudes de Sully's death in 1208 and was completed around the mid-1240s, and the two towers followed between 1225 and 1250.

In the mid-13th century the transepts were remodelled in the Rayonnant style: Jean de Chelles added a gabled portal and rose window to the north transept in the late 1240s, and Pierre de Montreuil did the same on the south from 1258. Pierre de Chelles, Jean Ravy, Jean le Bouteiller and Raymond du Temple later carried the work on. The date of the first flying buttresses is not known with precision; Andrew Tallon argued from laser scans that they were part of the original design, and the first buttresses were replaced by larger ones in the 14th century. Vault stones that fell in 2019 were quarried in the Vexin and presumably brought up the Seine by boat.
sections.reception:
Notre-Dame was already a public stage while building continued. Patriarch Heraclius of Jerusalem called for the Third Crusade from the still incomplete cathedral in 1185, and Philip the Fair opened the first Estates General there in 1302. In his Treatise on the Praises of Paris of 1323, John of Jandun named it one of the city's three most important buildings and wrote that it shone out "like the sun among stars". Saint Louis IX deposited there the relics of the Passion, including the crown of thorns, that he had bought from the Latin Emperor Baldwin II. On 16 December 1431 the boy-king Henry VI of England was crowned king of France in Notre-Dame, since Reims was under French control. During the late 12th and early 13th centuries it was the birthplace and leading centre of the Notre-Dame school of polyphony.

Tastes and use changed. In the Renaissance the Gothic style fell out of fashion and the pillars and walls were covered with tapestries. Rioting Huguenots damaged statues in 1548 as idolatrous. From 1630 the goldsmiths' guild donated a large altarpiece every year, the grands mays, and seventy-six had been given when the custom ended in 1708. In 1699 a major redecoration in the Louis XIV style began, and in 1756 the canons judged the interior too dark and had the medieval stained glass, except the roses, replaced with plain white panes.
sections.survival:
After 1789 Notre-Dame was seized as public property. It was rededicated in 1793 to the Cult of Reason and in 1794 to the Cult of the Supreme Being, and many treasures were destroyed or plundered. The twenty-eight statues of biblical kings on the west façade, mistaken for statues of French kings, were beheaded; many of the heads were found in a 1977 excavation and are displayed in the Musée de Cluny. The building was used as a warehouse. The Concordat of 1801 returned it to the Catholic Church, and the exterior was whitewashed and the interior decorated in Neoclassical style for Napoleon's coronation in 1804.

In the decades after the Napoleonic Wars it fell into such disrepair that Paris officials considered demolishing it. From 1844 Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc restored it, remaking or adding decoration that Viollet-le-Duc felt was in the spirit of the original style, including a taller and more ornate flèche; the work cost over 12 million francs. In May 1871 the Communards piled furniture to burn the cathedral but halted when they realised the fire would also destroy the neighbouring Hôtel-Dieu hospital. The façade was cleaned in 1963, and a renovation began in 1991 to replace weathered exterior stonework.
sections.legacy:
Victor Hugo wrote the novel Notre-Dame de Paris, published in English as The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, in 1831 to save the cathedral; it was an enormous success and raised awareness of its decay. Notre-Dame hosted the funerals of many presidents of the French Republic, and on 26 August 1944 a special Mass celebrated the liberation of Paris. In 1805 Pope Pius VII gave it the status of a minor basilica. Since 1905, like the other cathedrals of France, it has been owned by the French government, with the exclusive right of use granted to the Catholic Church. It is widely recognised as a symbol of both Paris and the French nation.

After the fire of 15 April 2019 President Emmanuel Macron promised that it would be restored. Heritage academics and professionals criticised a plan to build a new flèche quickly, and over 1,170 experts signed an open letter against exempting the cathedral from heritage law. A new flèche was put in place on 16 December 2023, and the cathedral reopened on 7 December 2024. Controversy continued over a plan to replace six undamaged 19th-century windows by Viollet-le-Duc with designs by Claire Tabouret; preservationists opposed it, and 140,000 people signed a petition to keep the old windows.

summary: Notre-Dame de Paris, begun in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and largely complete by 1260, is a Gothic cathedral known for its rib vaults, flying buttresses and rose windows. It was damaged in the Revolution, restored by Viollet-le-Duc, burned in 2019 and reopened in 2024.
notes: The article dates the Pillar of the Boatmen's discovery to 1710 in History and to 1711 in Burials and crypts; the year is left out.
The article says the great bells escaped being melted down in the Revolution, and elsewhere that most of the cathedral's bells were removed and melted down; bells in the Revolution are left out.

The south rose window is said to have been rebuilt 1725-1727 and rebuilt by Viollet-le-Duc in 1854 (key dates) or 1861 (windows section); left out. Choir completion is 1177 or 1182/1185 in different places; given as the article's 1177 (Robert of Torigni) and 1182 altar.

The north tower is given as 1235-1250 and the towers as 1225-1250; the latter used. The article says damage to the south rose occurred in the 'French Revolution of 1830' (a July Revolution); left out.
Left out: visitor numbers, cost of the 2019-2024 restoration, attendees at the reopening, the sacristy, organ and clock details, burials, recent attacks and plots.
